---
title: "6000-yr APAL-Climate Regional Analysis"
author: "Alexis E Medina Valmaseda"
abstract: |
  This document is the executable record (Quarto/R) of all analyses reported in the
  main text. It uses three input files deposited in the repository: `ages_kernel_reg_updt2.xlsx`
  (dated *Acropora palmata* fossils, audited against the original age publications),
  `df_GAM130326_regimes_v4.xlsx` (centennial climate predictors) and `Marine20_0-15ka.csv`
  (the Marine20 radiocarbon calibration curve, used to propagate age uncertainty). From these it reproduces:

  1. binning of fossil ages into 0.1-ka (centennial) intervals, their alignment with
     climate predictors and the normalization of the response variable;
  2. kernel-density reconstructions of *A. palmata* age distributions for each reef
     site and for the regional composite, weighted so that they have the shape of the
     modelled series;
  3. exploratory analyses of predictor correlation and of abundance across
     climate-regime combinations;
  4. beta-regression generalized additive models (GAMs) fitted separately to four reef
     sites (Punta Maroma, Florida, Belize, Saint Croix) and to a regional composite,
     first with one climate predictor at a time (marginal models) and then as a nested
     sequence of multi-predictor models, ranked by AIC and Akaike weights;
  5. diagnostics of the selected models (residual plots, concurvity, residual temporal
     autocorrelation) and sensitivity analyses;
  6. validation and robustness tests of the selected models (cross-validation against an
     s(age)-only reference model, circular-shift test, drop-one influence).

  Code, outputs and a factual description of each result are shown together, so that
  every value reported in the main text can be traced to the code that produced it.
  Ecological interpretation is given in the main text.
format: html
execute:
  echo: true
---

# REGIONAL ACROPORA PALMATA ANALYSIS

We import the fossil chronology (`ages_kernel_reg_updt2.xlsx`, sheet `Registros`) and retain *A. palmata* records (`group == "palmata"`) dated 0–6 ka. The site colours defined here (`custom_colors`) are used in all figures.

**Age reference, calibration and data corrections.** The chronology was audited record by record against the original publications of each age (workbook `coral_ages_audit_M3.xlsx`; sheet `Trazabilidad` of `ages_kernel_reg_updt2.xlsx` lists, for every record, its source, method, published age, analytical uncertainty, calibration and the change with respect to the previous version, `ages_kernel_reg_updt.xlsx`). All ages are expressed in ka BP (before 1950 CE), the reference of the climate series, and all radiocarbon ages are calibrated with Marine20 using a local reservoir correction (ΔR), propagated in quadrature.

- **Punta Maroma.** U-Th ages (Medina-Valmaseda et al. 2025) are published relative to the year of chemical separation (2021) and are converted to BP (0.071 ka younger). Ages from Blanchon et al. (2017) were already in years BP. One sample (SURF7(a), \~1956 CE) post-dates 1950; it keeps its age (−0.006 ka) and is assigned to the youngest bin. Two samples dated on separate subsamples (M1(a), M5(b)) retain both ages.

- **Saint Croix.** Radiocarbon ages (Hubbard et al. 2005, 2013), originally calibrated with Marine98 and no local correction, are recalibrated with Marine20 and ΔR = 64 ± 32 ¹⁴C yr (DiNapoli et al. 2020). For samples without a published conventional age (Hubbard et al. 2013), the conventional age and its uncertainty are recovered as the values that reproduce the published calibrated age and 2σ range under the original calibration. One sample dated at two laboratories (BI2-05) enters once, with the error-weighted mean of its conventional ages; one published calibrated age inconsistent with its conventional age (BI1-13) is replaced by the recalibrated value; samples listed in both source publications are counted once. Four U-Th ages are not modified.

- **Belize.** U-Th ages (Gischler et al. 2023) are in years BP and are not modified. Radiocarbon ages are recalibrated with Marine20 and ΔR = −248 ± 35 ¹⁴C yr (Greer et al. 2020), from the conventional ages in Gischler & Hudson (2004) or, for the atoll cores, from conventional ages recovered by inverting the original Marine98 calibration. Because this ΔR is a single, strongly negative estimate, we repeated the analysis using a regional ΔR of −114 ± 70 ¹⁴C yr (inverse-variance weighted mean of the ten nearest entries of the Marine Reservoir Database, with their standard deviation as uncertainty). Seven *A. cervicornis* samples previously coded as *A. palmata* were reclassified and excluded from the *A. palmata* series, and one typographical error in the compiled table was corrected from the original publication.

- **Florida.** Radiocarbon ages were recalibrated with Marine20 by L. T. Toth (pers. comm.), and three samples absent from that compilation were recalibrated with the same local correction. U-Th ages were already in years BP. Seventeen rows that repeated a sample already present under another source database were removed. Records were standardized by collection (main reef tract, nearshore ridge, Dry Tortugas) as before.

- **Effect.** *A. palmata* records in 0–6 ka: 257 → 236 (Punta Maroma 64, Florida 111, Belize 39, Saint Croix 22). Radiocarbon ages carry 95 % calibrated ranges of 0.3–0.5 kyr (3–5 centennial bins), so for the radiocarbon-dated sites the 0.1-kyr bin is an aggregation unit, not the resolving power of the records.

- **Calibration curve and age uncertainty.** The age uncertainty shown in Fig. 2 is computed within this document, not taken from the source publications: the Marine20 curve (Heaton et al. 2020; https://doi.org/10.1017/RDC.2020.68), deposited in the repository as `Marine20_0-15ka.csv` (0–15,000 cal BP, columns cal BP, ¹⁴C age and its 1σ error), is combined with the conventional age, its error and the local ΔR with its error of each radiocarbon age (sheet `Trazabilidad`) to obtain its calibrated probability distribution, from which the ages are drawn (Section 1.4). No external calibration software is needed to reproduce it.

<!-- Verificar antes de citar: DiNapoli et al. 2020, Greer et al. 2020. Heaton et al. 2020 = Marine20, Radiocarbon 62: 779–820. -->

```{r datos-reg}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev.args = list(pointsize = 15))   # base-graphics text +3 pt; ggplot text sizes are set in each theme
rm(list=ls(all=TRUE))
gc()
#install.packages("here")
library(here)
here()
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stargazer)

set.seed(20260930)
datos_reg <- read_excel(here("ages_kernel_reg_updt2.xlsx"), sheet = "Registros")

datos_reg_pal <- datos_reg %>%
  # post-1950 ages (t_ka < 0) enter the youngest bin
  filter(group == "palmata", t_ka > -0.1 & t_ka <= 6)

custom_colors <- c(
  "Punta Maroma" = "#F2941A",
  "Regional (All spots)" = "#4D4D4D",
  "Regional"             = "#4D4D4D",
  "Saint Croix" = "#CC79A7",
  "Belize" = "#7D9E5F",
  "Florida" = "#0072B2"
)
```

Each record is assigned to a 0.1-ka bin (right-closed intervals; the first interval includes 0), and the upper bound of the bin (`interval_max`) is stored as its centennial age. A second copy of all records is labelled "Regional", and the two sets are stacked into `centennial_counts_all`. This object is still record-level (one row per dated fossil); counts per bin are computed in later chunks.

```{r cent-count}
library(dplyr)

breaks <- seq(0, 6, by = 0.1)

datos_reg_pal <- datos_reg %>%
  # post-1950 ages (t_ka < 0) enter the youngest bin
  filter(group == "palmata", t_ka > -0.1 & t_ka <= 6)

centennial_counts_sites <- datos_reg_pal %>%
  mutate(interval_bin = cut(
    pmax(t_ka, 0),
    breaks = breaks,
    include.lowest = TRUE,
    right = TRUE
  )) %>%
  mutate(interval_max = breaks[match(interval_bin, levels(interval_bin)) + 1])

centennial_counts_regional <- datos_reg %>%
  # post-1950 ages (t_ka < 0) enter the youngest bin
  filter(group == "palmata", t_ka > -0.1 & t_ka <= 6) %>%
  mutate(interval_bin = cut(
    pmax(t_ka, 0),
    breaks = breaks,
    include.lowest = TRUE,
    right = TRUE
  )) %>%
  mutate(
    spot = "Regional",
    interval_max = breaks[match(interval_bin, levels(interval_bin)) + 1]
  )

centennial_counts_all <- bind_rows(centennial_counts_sites, centennial_counts_regional)
```

## *1. Data Overview*

### 1.1 Summary of fossil records by site

We summarize the raw record-level ages by site (**Supplementary Table S1**): number of records, mean, SD, minimum and maximum age. `min_interval` and `max_interval` give the upper bound of the bins containing the youngest and oldest record.

```{r count-summ}
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(gt)
library(stringr)

tabla_resumen_counts <- centennial_counts_all %>%
  group_by(spot) %>%
  summarise(
    n_records   = n(),                               
    mean_t_ka   = mean(t_ka, na.rm = TRUE),         
    sd_t_ka     = sd(t_ka, na.rm = TRUE),           
    min_t_ka    = min(t_ka, na.rm = TRUE),          
    max_t_ka    = max(t_ka, na.rm = TRUE),          
    min_interval = interval_max[which.min(t_ka)],   
    max_interval = interval_max[which.max(t_ka)],   
    .groups = "drop"  ) %>%
  arrange(spot)


tab_S1 <- tabla_resumen_counts %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Summary of fossil records by site (raw data)",
    subtitle = "Temporal distribution and dispersion per 0.1 ka bin"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(mean_t_ka, sd_t_ka, min_t_ka, max_t_ka,
                min_interval, max_interval),
    decimals = 3
  )

tab_S1
gt::gtsave(tab_S1, "Supplementary_Table_S1.docx")   
```

The dataset comprises 236 dated records: Florida 111, Punta Maroma 64, Belize 39 and Saint Croix 22. Mean ages range from 2.20 ka (Punta Maroma) to 3.56 ka (Florida). Punta Maroma records span −0.006 ka (one post-1950 colony, assigned to the youngest bin) to 5.46 ka, Belize 0–5.54 ka, Saint Croix 0.073–5.81 ka and Florida 0.069–6.00 ka.

### 1.2 Climatic predictor: import & alignment

We import the centennial climate table (`df_GAM130326_regimes_v4.xlsx`) and assign each row the upper bound of its 0.1-ka bin. Ages are in ka BP (before 1950 CE), the convention of the two continuous climate sources (Kaufman et al. 2020; Schmitt et al. 2025).

**Variables of the climate table.** `GMHT_CPS0_30N`: temperature anomaly of the Composite Plus Scale reconstruction for 0°–30°N (°C; Kaufman et al. 2020). `dT_raw`: its centennial rate of change (δT), the difference between consecutive 0.1-ka bins (°C per century). `Hur100_fqcy`: centennial tropical-cyclone (TC) frequency, the number of TC event layers in each 0.1-ka bin of the Great Blue Hole record (Schmitt et al. 2025). `Hur100_av`: smoothed centennial TC frequency, the mean of the two 100-year counts of the same record that overlap the bin (a centred 200-year smoothing). Both metrics count tropical storms and hurricanes; neither measures intensity. Schmitt et al. (2025, table S9) count events in windows of varve years before 2022 CE, so both metrics were recounted in our BP bins from their 50- and 100-year windows (a BP bin *j* spans 72 + 100*j* to 72 + 100(*j* + 1) years before 2022). As with the coral ages (Section 1.1), the youngest bin closes at the youngest dated colony (1956 CE): `Hur100_fqcy` counts 1850–1956 CE (15 events, one of them in 1956), and `Hur100_av` averages the windows 1800–1900 and 1900–2000 CE. Events after 2000 CE, including the 21st-century extrapolation of 45 events per century, are not used. The rebuild is documented bin by bin in sheet `Hur_BP_traceability` of the climate table; the earlier table (`df_GAM130326_regimes_v3.xlsx`) took the windows counted from 2022 CE in order, as if they were BP bins, which placed the counts about 150 years from the BP bins, and it had 45 events in the youngest bin. Counts recomputed from the individual event layers (Schmitt et al. 2025, table S4a) agree with the rebuilt series (*r* = 0.99; at most 2 events per bin apart). A sensitivity version that extends the youngest bin to 2022 CE as a rate per century (`df_GAM130326_regimes_v4c.xlsx`) is described in Section 4.7.1. `Thermal`, `Hydro` and `Hurricane`: categorical regimes (below). `Hydro_FL`, `Hur_FL`, `FL_pact` and `FL_nrec`: Florida series (below).

The three categorical regimes were coded from the published chronologies compiled in Supplementary Material 2, converted to ka BP, assigning each bin to the period that contains its midpoint (a midpoint on a boundary goes to the younger period):

- **Thermal** (published chronology, not the GMST series): warmer 0–0.1 ka (post-1850 CE); LIA 0.1–0.7 ka (\~1300–1850 CE); CWP&MWA 0.7–1.3 ka (700–1250 CE); cooler 1.3–4.8 ka; warmer 4.8–6.0 ka (mid-Holocene warmth).
- **Hurricane** (Schmitt et al. 2025 only, the source of `Hur100_av` and `Hur100_fqcy`): high 0–0.2 ka (rise after 1800 CE); calm 0.2–0.6 ka (1400–1800 CE); enhanced 0.6–1.1 and 1.2–1.4 ka (900–1400 and 600–800 CE); moderate 1.1–1.2 and 1.4–4.0 ka (mean 9–14 events per century); low 4.0–6.0 ka (\~7 events per century; the record begins at 5.7 ka).
- **Hydro**, by region. Yucatán (`Hydro`): wet 0–0.8 ka, dry 0.8–1.7 ka and wet 1.7–3.5 ka (Curtis et al. 1996, boundaries calibrated with IntCal20), wet 5.2–5.7 ka (Serrato Marks et al. 2021), no data elsewhere. Florida (`Hydro_FL`): dry 4.6–6.0 ka (Pollock et al. 2017; Donders 2014), wet 2.8–4.6 ka and dry 0–2.8 ka (Glaser et al. 2013), with multi-century droughts near 1.0 and 0.4 ka (Willard & Bernhardt 2011).
- **Hurricane, Florida** (`Hur_FL`, `FL_pact`, `FL_nrec`). Schmitt et al. (2025) record storms reaching the Yucatán coast, and Florida-proximal records do not follow it (agreement in 34 % of the bins younger than 3.5 ka). The Florida panel therefore uses a local series built from six records on the Atlantic side of Florida: the western Great Bahama Bank / Florida Straits (Toomey et al. 2013; 0–6 ka), the Everglades (Yao et al. 2020; 0–3.5 ka), southwest Florida (Ercolani et al., via Oliva et al. 2017), Andros and Abaco (van Hengstum et al., via Oliva et al. 2017) and Abaco (Winkler et al. 2020). All ages are cal BP (1950). For each bin, `FL_pact` is the proportion of the records covering the bin that report an active interval at its midpoint, `FL_nrec` the number of those records, and `Hur_FL` is "active" when `FL_pact` ≥ 0.5 and "quiet" otherwise. Older than 3.5 ka the series rests on a single record (Toomey et al. 2013). Records from the Gulf coast of Florida were not used, because they sample Gulf landfalls. For Hydro and the hurricane regime, the Florida panel uses the Florida series; Punta Maroma, Belize, Saint Croix and the regional composite use the Yucatán series (Hurricane = Schmitt et al. 2025). The continuous hurricane metrics (`Hur100_av`, `Hur100_fqcy`) are those of Schmitt et al. (2025) in every panel. In the Yucatán Hydro series, undocumented bins are coded as a separate level, "no data", so that no bins are lost. The mapping is positional: `interval_max` is taken from the order in which interval labels first appear, which is correct only if the file has exactly one row per bin, ordered from youngest to oldest.

Climate values are joined to every fossil record by `interval_max`, and the column is renamed `age` (ka). The resulting `merged_df` is record-level and therefore holds climate values only for bins that contain at least one fossil record.

```{r data-integ}
datos_cli <- read_excel(here("df_GAM130326_regimes_v4.xlsx"))
datos_cli<-as.data.frame(datos_cli)

library(dplyr)

breaks <- seq(0, 6, by = 0.1)

datos_cli <- datos_cli %>%
  mutate(interval = factor(interval, levels = unique(interval))) %>%
  mutate(interval_max = breaks[match(interval, levels(interval)) + 1])

datos_cli <- datos_cli %>%
  mutate(Hydro_YUC = ifelse(is.na(Hydro), "no data", Hydro))

# Hydro and hurricane regime by region: Florida records take the Florida series,
# all other records the Yucatán series (Hurricane = Schmitt et al. 2025)
merged_df <- centennial_counts_all %>%
  left_join(datos_cli, by = "interval_max") %>%
  mutate(Hydro     = ifelse(spot == "Florida", Hydro_FL, Hydro_YUC),
         Hurricane = ifelse(spot == "Florida", Hur_FL, Hurricane)) %>%
  select(-Hydro_FL, -Hydro_YUC, -Hur_FL, -FL_nrec) %>%
  rename( age = interval_max)
```

### 1.3 Response variable: centennial counts and normalization

The response variable of all models is built here, before any figure, so that Figs. 2 and 3 show the same series that enter the GAMs. This chunk makes three lasting changes to `merged_df`:

1.  **Reference levels.** Thermal, Hydro and Hurricane are converted to factors with reference levels "warmer", "wet" and "low" ("quiet" for the local Florida hurricane series). These levels carry through the aggregation below and define every categorical contrast reported in Sections 3.2 and 3.3.

2.  **Sites only.** Rows are restricted to the four reef sites, which drops the duplicated "Regional" records created in the binning step. The regional composite is rebuilt from the site series below.

3.  **Record counter.** A column `counts = 1` is added (one per dated record); it is summed per bin below.

```         
The per-site objects (`datos_pm`, `datos_fl`, `datos_bz`, `datos_sc`, `datos_reg`) and `merged_df_g` created in this chunk are intermediate: all of them are redefined below, before any model is fitted.
```

```{r data-prepa}
library(mgcv)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)

merged_df <- merged_df %>%
  mutate(
    Thermal   = relevel(as.factor(Thermal), ref = "warmer"),
    Hydro     = relevel(as.factor(Hydro), ref = "wet"),
    # "low" is the reference of the Schmitt regimes; in Florida (local series) the
    # first level present, "quiet", is the reference
    Hurricane = factor(Hurricane, levels = c("low", "moderate", "calm", "enhanced", "high",
                                             "quiet", "active"))
  )%>%
  filter(spot %in% c("Punta Maroma", "Florida", "Belize", "Saint Croix")) %>%
  mutate(panel = spot)

datos_pm <- merged_df %>% filter(spot == "Punta Maroma")
datos_fl <- merged_df %>% filter(spot == "Florida")
datos_bz <- merged_df %>% filter(spot == "Belize")
datos_sc <- merged_df %>% filter(spot == "Saint Croix")
datos_reg <- merged_df %>%
  filter(spot %in% c("Punta Maroma", "Florida", "Belize", "Saint Croix")) %>%
  mutate(spot = "Regional")

merged_df <- merged_df %>%
   mutate(counts = 1)

merged_df_g <- bind_rows(datos_pm, datos_fl, datos_bz, datos_sc, datos_reg)

```

#### Normalization

For each site, records are summed per bin (`counts`). Climate predictors are averaged within the bin, which leaves them unchanged because they are constant within a bin; regime labels are taken from the first record in the bin.

`normalize_counts()` divides counts by the site maximum (`counts_norm`, rounded to four decimals). Values exactly 0 or 1 are then transformed as y′ = (y(*n* − 1) + 0.5)/*n*, where *n* is the number of bins in the series (`counts_norm_sv`); all other values are unchanged. Only bins containing at least one record exist in the series, so no zeros occur and the correction affects only the maximum bin (e.g. 0.984 in Punta Maroma, *n* = 31).

The response is therefore the relative abundance within bins in which a site is represented. Bins without records are not part of any model: 29 of 60 in Punta Maroma, 36 in Belize, 41 in Saint Croix, 16 in Florida and 3 in the regional composite.

#### Florida source standardization

Florida combines records from several source datasets (column `source`). Counts are therefore first summed per source and bin, divided by the maximum of each source and boundary-corrected; the standardized values are then summed across sources per bin and normalized as above (`datos_fl_std`). Each source thus has equal weight at its maximum, independent of its number of records.

The regional composite used in every model is the per-bin sum of the four site-level `counts_norm_sv` series (Florida in its source-standardized form), normalized with the same function (`datos_reg`, *n* = 57 bins). Each site therefore enters the composite with its maximum bin equal to one, so its contribution depends on how its records are distributed among bins rather than on its number of records (Section 1.4). The five series are stacked into `merged_df_g`, which is used by every model and by Figs. 2 and 3a.

```{r norm-stand}

normalize_counts <- function(df, panel_name){
  
  df %>%
    mutate(
      counts_norm = round(
        counts / max(counts, na.rm = TRUE),
        4
      ),
      
      counts_norm_sv = ifelse(
        counts_norm %in% c(0,1),
        ((counts_norm * (n() - 1)) + 0.5) / n(),
        counts_norm
      ),
      
      panel = panel_name
    )
  
}

#---------------------------------------------------------
# PUNTA MAROMA
#---------------------------------------------------------

datos_pm <- merged_df %>%
  filter(spot == "Punta Maroma") %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(
    counts = sum(counts, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_av = mean(Hur100_av, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_fqcy = mean(Hur100_fqcy, na.rm = TRUE),
    GMHT_CPS0_30N = mean(GMHT_CPS0_30N, na.rm = TRUE),
    dT_raw = mean(dT_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hydro = first(Hydro),
    Thermal = first(Thermal),
    Hurricane = first(Hurricane),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  normalize_counts("Punta Maroma")

#---------------------------------------------------------
# BELIZE
#---------------------------------------------------------

datos_bz <- merged_df %>%
  filter(spot == "Belize") %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(
    counts = sum(counts, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_av = mean(Hur100_av, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_fqcy = mean(Hur100_fqcy, na.rm = TRUE),
    GMHT_CPS0_30N = mean(GMHT_CPS0_30N, na.rm = TRUE),
    dT_raw = mean(dT_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hydro = first(Hydro),
    Thermal = first(Thermal),
    Hurricane = first(Hurricane),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  normalize_counts("Belize")

#---------------------------------------------------------
# SAINT CROIX
#---------------------------------------------------------

datos_sc <- merged_df %>%
  filter(spot == "Saint Croix") %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(
    counts = sum(counts, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_av = mean(Hur100_av, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_fqcy = mean(Hur100_fqcy, na.rm = TRUE),
    GMHT_CPS0_30N = mean(GMHT_CPS0_30N, na.rm = TRUE),
    dT_raw = mean(dT_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hydro = first(Hydro),
    Thermal = first(Thermal),
    Hurricane = first(Hurricane),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  normalize_counts("Saint Croix")

#---------------------------------------------------------
# FLORIDA
# Independently standardized by source dataset 
#---------------------------------------------------------

datos_fl_std <- merged_df %>%
  filter(spot == "Florida") %>%
  
  group_by(source, age) %>%
  summarise(
    counts = sum(counts, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    Hur100_av = mean(Hur100_av, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_fqcy = mean(Hur100_fqcy, na.rm = TRUE),
    GMHT_CPS0_30N = mean(GMHT_CPS0_30N, na.rm = TRUE),
    dT_raw = mean(dT_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hydro = first(Hydro),
    Thermal = first(Thermal),
    Hurricane = first(Hurricane),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  
  group_by(source) %>%
  mutate(
    
    counts_std = counts / max(counts, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    counts_std = ifelse(
      counts_std %in% c(0,1),
      ((counts_std * (n() - 1)) + 0.5) / n(),
      counts_std
    )
    
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(
    
    counts = sum(counts_std, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    Hur100_av = mean(Hur100_av, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_fqcy = mean(Hur100_fqcy, na.rm = TRUE),
    GMHT_CPS0_30N = mean(GMHT_CPS0_30N, na.rm = TRUE),
    dT_raw = mean(dT_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    Hydro = first(Hydro),
    Thermal = first(Thermal),
    Hurricane = first(Hurricane),
    
    .groups = "drop"
    
  ) %>%
  normalize_counts("Florida")

#---------------------------------------------------------
# REGIONAL
# build upon normalized datasets
#---------------------------------------------------------

datos_reg <- bind_rows(
  datos_pm,
  datos_fl_std,
  datos_bz,
  datos_sc
) %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(
    
    counts = sum(counts_norm_sv, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    Hur100_av = mean(Hur100_av, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_fqcy = mean(Hur100_fqcy, na.rm = TRUE),
    GMHT_CPS0_30N = mean(GMHT_CPS0_30N, na.rm = TRUE),
    dT_raw = mean(dT_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    Hydro = first(Hydro),
    Thermal = first(Thermal),
    Hurricane = first(Hurricane),
    
    .groups = "drop"
    
  ) %>%
  select(-Hydro) %>%
  left_join(datos_cli %>% transmute(age = interval_max, Hydro = Hydro_YUC, Hur_YUC = Hurricane),
            by = "age") %>%
  mutate(Hydro = factor(Hydro, levels = levels(merged_df$Hydro)),
         Hurricane = factor(Hur_YUC, levels = levels(merged_df$Hurricane))) %>%
  select(-Hur_YUC) %>%
  normalize_counts("Regional")

#---------------------------------------------------------
# Ready-to use dataset
#---------------------------------------------------------

merged_df_g <- bind_rows(
  datos_pm,
  datos_fl_std,
  datos_bz,
  datos_sc,
  datos_reg
)
```

### 1.4 *Acropora palmata* age densities (weighted KDE)

Kernel density estimates (KDE) are computed from the individual ages, weighted so that the density has the shape of the modelled series of Section 1.3. Each record receives the weight it carries in `counts_norm_sv`: in Punta Maroma, Belize and Saint Croix, `counts_norm_sv / counts` of its bin; in Florida, the product of its source-standardization factor and the Florida normalization factor; in the regional composite, the site weight multiplied by the regional normalization factor. The weights of the records in each bin therefore add up to `counts_norm_sv` of that bin (checked in the code). For a site with a single source the weights are constant except in the maximum bin, so the weighted KDE has the same shape as the KDE of the raw ages; the weighting changes the shape only for Florida (source standardization) and for the regional composite.

Each density is a Gaussian KDE over 0–6 ka (bandwidth 0.09 ka, 512 points) with a reflection boundary correction (Silverman 1986; Jones 1993): ages are mirrored at 0 and 6 ka, so that the part of each kernel that would fall outside the window is folded back into it. Without the correction the density is underestimated within about two bandwidths of each edge, by up to one half at the edge itself, which would understate the modern peak and the abundance of the oldest centuries; with it each curve integrates to one over 0–6 ka. Post-1950 ages count at 0 ka, as in the binning. The bandwidth is a smoothing choice, not the resolving power of the record: the 95 % range of a radiocarbon age spans 0.3–0.5 ka (3–5 centennial bins), that of a U-Th age 0.02–0.05 ka. Two sources of uncertainty are estimated separately:

- **Sampling** (which fossils were recovered and dated): 1,000 bootstrap resamples of the records with replacement, keeping their weights and stratified by source in Florida and by site in the regional composite. For each resample we keep the density curve and its mean in each 0.1-ka bin. `signal_all` holds the estimate and the 2.5–97.5 % and 25–75 % bootstrap envelopes of each curve; `centennial_density_all` holds the bin means of the estimate and their bootstrap SD and 95 % interval.
- **Age** (where each dated fossil falls in time): 1,000 Monte Carlo draws of every age, with the record weights held at their central values; draws older than 6 ka leave the window. U-Th ages are drawn from a normal distribution with SD equal to half the reported 2σ error. Radiocarbon ages are drawn from their calibrated probability distribution, computed here from the conventional age, its error and the local ΔR with its error (combined in quadrature) under Marine20 (Heaton et al. 2020; https://doi.org/10.1017/RDC.2020.68; curve deposited as `Marine20_0-15ka.csv`), and shifted so that its median equals the audited age (the shift is ≤ 1 yr except for a few Florida ages calibrated with other software by their authors). The inputs are read from the sheet `Trazabilidad` of `ages_kernel_reg_updt2.xlsx`. Three Florida radiocarbon ages without a ΔR error take the median ΔR error of Florida. The 2.5–97.5 % range of the draws is the age envelope (`age_q025`, `age_q975` in `signal_all`) and the 95 % range of each age is shown in Fig. 2.

Because a KDE integrates to one, the regional density distributes a fixed total among the four sites in proportion to the sum of their weights, which depends on how their records are spread among bins, not on how many records they have. Saint Croix, whose 22 records occupy 19 bins with at most two records each, carries 26 % of the regional weight with 9 % of the records, and Punta Maroma 12 % with 27 % of the records (`site_share`). This is a property of the per-site normalization used in the models, not of the KDE, and it applies equally to the regional GAMs.

```{r dens}
library(dplyr)
library(gt)

## ---- record-level weights reproducing the modelled response -------------------
## The weights of the records in a bin add up to counts_norm_sv of that bin, so the
## weighted KDE has the shape of the series that enter the GAMs.
bin_upper <- function(t) breaks[as.integer(cut(pmax(t, 0), breaks, include.lowest = TRUE, right = TRUE)) + 1]

recs <- datos_reg_pal %>%
  mutate(t_ka = as.numeric(t_ka), age = round(bin_upper(t_ka), 1))

# Punta Maroma, Belize, Saint Croix: weight = counts_norm_sv / counts of the bin
w_single <- bind_rows(datos_pm, datos_bz, datos_sc) %>%
  transmute(spot = panel, age = round(age, 1), w_site = counts_norm_sv / counts)

# Florida: per-source standardization (as in datos_fl_std), then the Florida normalization
w_fl_src <- recs %>%
  filter(spot == "Florida") %>%
  count(source, age, name = "n_src") %>%
  group_by(source) %>%
  mutate(std = n_src / max(n_src),
         std = ifelse(std %in% c(0, 1), (std * (n() - 1) + 0.5) / n(), std),
         w_src = std / n_src) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(source, age, w_src)
w_fl_bin <- datos_fl_std %>% transmute(age = round(age, 1), w_bin = counts_norm_sv / counts)

# Regional composite: site weights rescaled by the regional normalization
w_reg_bin <- datos_reg %>% transmute(age = round(age, 1), w_reg = counts_norm_sv / counts)

recs <- recs %>%
  left_join(w_single, by = c("spot", "age")) %>%
  left_join(w_fl_src, by = c("source", "age")) %>%
  left_join(w_fl_bin, by = "age") %>%
  left_join(w_reg_bin, by = "age") %>%
  mutate(w_site = ifelse(spot == "Florida", w_src * w_bin, w_site),
         w_regional = w_site * w_reg) %>%
  select(-w_src, -w_bin, -w_reg)

# check: the weights of each bin reproduce the modelled series
chk_site <- recs %>% group_by(spot, age) %>% summarise(w = sum(w_site), .groups = "drop") %>%
  inner_join(bind_rows(datos_pm, datos_fl_std, datos_bz, datos_sc) %>%
               transmute(spot = panel, age = round(age, 1), y = counts_norm_sv), by = c("spot", "age"))
chk_reg <- recs %>% group_by(age) %>% summarise(w = sum(w_regional), .groups = "drop") %>%
  inner_join(datos_reg %>% transmute(age = round(age, 1), y = counts_norm_sv), by = "age")
stopifnot(nrow(chk_site) == sum(merged_df_g$panel != "Regional"),
          nrow(chk_reg) == sum(merged_df_g$panel == "Regional"),
          max(abs(chk_site$w - chk_site$y)) < 1e-3, max(abs(chk_reg$w - chk_reg$y)) < 1e-3)

# share of each site in the regional density (weights sum to one)
site_share <- recs %>% group_by(spot) %>%
  summarise(records = n(), pct_records = 100 * n() / nrow(recs),
            pct_weight = 100 * sum(w_regional) / sum(recs$w_regional), .groups = "drop")
site_share

## ---- weighted KDE with stratified bootstrap -------------------------------------
## Records are resampled with replacement within strata (sources in Florida, sites in the
## regional composite), keeping their weights. bw = 0.09 ka, 512 points over 0-6 ka.
## Boundary correction by reflection (Silverman 1986; Jones 1993): ages are mirrored at
## 0 and 6 ka, so the kernel mass that would fall outside the window is folded back
## inside it. Without it the density is underestimated within ~2 bandwidths of each edge
## (by up to half at the edge itself). Output on 512 points over 0-6 ka.
## As in the binning, post-1950 ages (t < 0) count at 0 ka, and ages > 6 ka (Monte Carlo
## draws that leave the window) are dropped.
kde_reflect <- function(t, w, bw, n = 512) {
  keep <- t <= 6
  t <- pmax(t[keep], 0); w <- w[keep] / sum(w[keep])
  d <- density(c(t, -t, 12 - t), weights = rep(w, 3) / 3, bw = bw, from = 0, to = 6, n = n)
  d$y <- 3 * d$y
  d
}

calc_density_summary <- function(t, w, spot_name, strata = rep(1, length(t)),
                                 B = 1000, bw = 0.09) {
  kde <- function(i) kde_reflect(t[i], w[i], bw = bw)
  full <- kde(seq_along(t))
  idx  <- split(seq_along(t), strata)
  boot <- t(vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) {
    i <- unlist(lapply(idx, function(ix) ix[sample.int(length(ix), length(ix), replace = TRUE)]))
    kde(i)$y
  }, numeric(512)))

  signal_df <- data.frame(
    x = full$x, estimate = full$y,
    q025 = apply(boot, 2, quantile, 0.025), q975 = apply(boot, 2, quantile, 0.975),
    q25  = apply(boot, 2, quantile, 0.25),  q75  = apply(boot, 2, quantile, 0.75),
    spot = spot_name)

  # centennial summary: estimate and bootstrap SD of the bin-mean density
  bin <- cut(full$x, breaks = breaks, include.lowest = TRUE, right = TRUE)
  bin_mean <- function(y) tapply(y, bin, mean)
  boot_bins <- apply(boot, 1, bin_mean)                 # 60 bins x B
  centennial_summary <- data.frame(
    interval_mid = breaks[-length(breaks)] + 0.05,
    density      = as.numeric(bin_mean(full$y)),
    boot_sd      = apply(boot_bins, 1, sd),
    boot_q025    = apply(boot_bins, 1, quantile, 0.025),
    boot_q975    = apply(boot_bins, 1, quantile, 0.975),
    spot         = spot_name)

  list(signal_df = signal_df, centennial_summary = centennial_summary)
}

site_levels <- c("Punta Maroma", "Belize", "Saint Croix", "Florida")
results_list <- lapply(site_levels, function(sp) {
  r <- recs %>% filter(spot == sp)
  calc_density_summary(r$t_ka, r$w_site, sp,
                       strata = if (sp == "Florida") r$source else rep(1, nrow(r)))
})
results_list <- c(results_list, list(
  calc_density_summary(recs$t_ka, recs$w_regional, "Regional composite", strata = recs$spot)))

signal_all <- bind_rows(lapply(results_list, `[[`, "signal_df"))
centennial_density_all <- bind_rows(lapply(results_list, `[[`, "centennial_summary"))

## ---- Supplementary Table S2 ---------------------------------------------------
tabla_resumen <- centennial_density_all %>%
  mutate(spot = factor(spot, levels = c(site_levels, "Regional composite"))) %>%
  group_by(Site = spot) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_boot_sd  = mean(boot_sd),
    max_density   = max(density),
    max_interval  = interval_mid[which.max(density)],
    min_density   = min(density),
    min_interval  = interval_mid[which.min(density)],
    .groups = "drop")

tab_S2 <- tabla_resumen %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(title = "Centennial weighted kernel-density summaries by site",
             subtitle = "Density of the modelled series and its bootstrap uncertainty") %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(mean_boot_sd, max_density, min_density), decimals = 3) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(max_interval, min_interval), decimals = 2)
tab_S2
gt::gtsave(tab_S2, "Supplementary_Table_S2.docx")
```

**Supplementary Table S2. Centennial weighted kernel-density summaries.** For each site and the regional composite: mean bootstrap SD of the bin-mean density over the 60 bins (`mean_boot_sd`), and the maximum and minimum bin-mean density with the bin midpoint (ka) at which each occurs.

Maximum density occurs at 0.05 ka (the youngest bin) in Punta Maroma, Belize and the regional composite, at 0.85 ka in Saint Croix and at 5.95 ka in Florida, where many records fall at 5.8–6.0 ka. Minima fall at 5.95 ka (Punta Maroma), 2.45 ka (Belize and Saint Croix), 1.45 ka (Florida) and 0.45 ka (regional composite). With the audited ages the youngest bin holds the maximum of the regional curve with or without the weights.

**Intervals without records and low-density intervals.** Two kinds of interval are marked in Fig. 2, both computed from the audited ages:

- **Published presence gaps** (coloured bars) for Punta Maroma (Medina-Valmaseda et al., 2025) and Belize (Hubbard et al., 2005; Gischler et al., 2023). Each is drawn as the record-free interval of the audited ages that overlaps the published gap (`site_gaps`), so its limits follow the corrected chronology.
- **Low-density intervals** (grey shading), in every panel, including the regional composite, for which no gaps have been published: intervals of at least 0.2 ka in which the upper 95 % limits of both the sampling and the age envelopes stay below the density of a uniform distribution over 0–6 ka (1/6 per ka; dashed line). These are centuries with fewer records than expected under a uniform distribution of the dated fossils, irrespective of which fossils were dated and of their age uncertainty (`low_density`). The rule recovers independently the published gaps of Punta Maroma and Belize. In the regional composite it identifies a single interval, during the Little Ice Age; the regional intervals marked in the previous version (2.20–3.00 and 5.10–5.90 ka) do not meet it with the audited ages.

```{r fig2-uncert}
library(readxl)
## ---- record metadata (method, analytical uncertainty, calibration inputs) -------
## from the traceability sheet of the chronology, linked by record ID
trace <- read_excel(here("ages_kernel_reg_updt2.xlsx"), sheet = "Trazabilidad") %>%
  select(ID, method, err_2s_ka, conv14C, conv14C_err, dR, dR_err) %>%
  mutate(across(c(err_2s_ka, conv14C, conv14C_err, dR, dR_err), as.numeric))
recs <- recs %>% left_join(trace, by = "ID")
stopifnot(!any(is.na(recs$method)), !any(is.na(recs$err_2s_ka)))

## ---- age uncertainty: Monte Carlo draws of every age ------------------------------
## U-Th: normal, sd = 2-sigma error / 2. Radiocarbon: draws from the calibrated
## probability distribution (Marine20; conventional age, its error and the local dR,
## errors combined in quadrature), shifted so that its median equals the audited age
## (the shift is <= 1 yr except where the published calibration used other software).
## Three Florida 14C ages without a dR error take the median dR error of Florida.
m20  <- read.csv(here("Marine20_0-15ka.csv"), comment.char = "#")
g    <- 0:15000
m20_mu <- approx(m20$cal_BP, m20$c14_age, g)$y
m20_sd <- approx(m20$cal_BP, m20$sigma, g)$y
dre_fl <- median(recs$dR_err[recs$spot == "Florida" & recs$method == "14C"], na.rm = TRUE)

N_age <- 1000
draw_age <- function(i) {
  r <- recs[i, ]
  if (r$method != "14C") return(rnorm(N_age, r$t_ka, r$err_2s_ka / 2))
  dre <- ifelse(is.na(r$dR_err), dre_fl, r$dR_err)
  s2  <- r$conv14C_err^2 + dre^2 + m20_sd^2
  p   <- exp(-(r$conv14C - r$dR - m20_mu)^2 / (2 * s2)) / sqrt(s2)
  p   <- p / sum(p)
  med <- g[which(cumsum(p) >= 0.5)[1]]
  x   <- sample(g, N_age, replace = TRUE, prob = p) + runif(N_age, -0.5, 0.5)
  (x - med) / 1000 + r$t_ka
}
set.seed(20261003)
age_draws <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(recs)), draw_age, numeric(N_age)))   # records x draws

## 95 % range of each age (for the record panels)
recs <- recs %>%
  mutate(lo95 = apply(age_draws, 1, quantile, 0.025),
         hi95 = apply(age_draws, 1, quantile, 0.975))

## ---- weighted KDE under age uncertainty (weights held at their central values) ------
kde_age_env <- function(idx, w, bw = 0.09) {
  dens <- vapply(seq_len(N_age), function(j)
    kde_reflect(age_draws[idx, j], w, bw = bw)$y,
    numeric(512))
  data.frame(age_q025 = apply(dens, 1, quantile, 0.025),
             age_q975 = apply(dens, 1, quantile, 0.975))
}
age_env <- bind_rows(
  lapply(site_levels, function(sp) {
    i <- which(recs$spot == sp)
    cbind(spot = sp, x = signal_all$x[signal_all$spot == sp], kde_age_env(i, recs$w_site[i]))
  }),
  cbind(spot = "Regional composite", x = signal_all$x[signal_all$spot == "Regional composite"],
        kde_age_env(seq_len(nrow(recs)), recs$w_regional)))
signal_all <- signal_all %>% left_join(age_env, by = c("spot", "x"))

## ---- intervals without records -----------------------------------------------------
## Sites: the record-free interval of the audited ages that overlaps each published gap
## (Punta Maroma: Medina-Valmaseda et al. 2025; Belize: Hubbard et al. 2005, Gischler et al. 2023).
pub_gaps <- data.frame(spot = c("Punta Maroma", "Belize", "Belize", "Belize"),
                       pub_min = c(0.71, 1.99, 3.68, 5.54), pub_max = c(1.44, 2.72, 4.20, 6.00))
gap_from_records <- function(t, a, b) {
  e <- sort(unique(c(t, 6)))
  k <- which(head(e, -1) < b & tail(e, -1) > a)
  k <- k[which.max(diff(e)[k])]
  c(e[k], e[k + 1])
}
site_gaps <- pub_gaps %>% rowwise() %>%
  mutate(g = list(gap_from_records(recs$t_ka[recs$spot == spot], pub_min, pub_max)),
         xmin = g[1], xmax = g[2]) %>% ungroup() %>% select(-g)

## Regional composite: no published gaps. Low-density intervals are recalculated as the
## intervals (>= 0.2 ka) in which the upper 95 % limit of BOTH envelopes (sampling and age)
## stays below the density of a uniform distribution over 0-6 ka (1/6 per ka).
low_runs <- function(x, flag, min_len = 0.2) {
  r <- rle(flag); end <- cumsum(r$lengths); start <- end - r$lengths + 1
  out <- data.frame(xmin = x[start], xmax = x[end])[r$values, , drop = FALSE]
  out[out$xmax - out$xmin >= min_len, , drop = FALSE]
}
low_density <- bind_rows(lapply(c(site_levels, "Regional composite"), function(sp) {
  d <- signal_all %>% filter(spot == sp)
  cbind(spot = sp, low_runs(d$x, pmax(d$q975, d$age_q975) < 1 / 6))
}))
reg_gaps <- low_density %>% filter(spot == "Regional composite")

site_gaps
low_density
```

**Figure 2** (`Figure_2.pdf`). *Acropora palmata* age distributions and their uncertainty. (a–d) Each site: weighted kernel density (bandwidth 0.09 ka, reflection-corrected at 0 and 6 ka; line) with its 95 % sampling envelope (bootstrap of the records; light) and 95 % age envelope (Monte Carlo of the ages; dark); below, every dated fossil with its 95 % age range, by dating method (circles U-Th, triangles ¹⁴C). (e) Regional composite. Dashed horizontal line (every panel): density expected if the dated fossils were spread evenly over 0–6 ka (uniform distribution, 1/6 ≈ 0.17 ka⁻¹), the reference used to define the low-density intervals. Grey shading: low-density intervals (both upper 95 % limits below the uniform density). Coloured bars: published presence gaps, bounded by the audited ages. In Punta Maroma (U-Th only) the age envelope is narrower than the line at this scale: its chronology is effectively fixed and its uncertainty is almost entirely sampling. Where the age envelope is as wide as the sampling envelope (Saint Croix, dated only by radiocarbon), the timing of density peaks and troughs is not resolved at the centennial scale.

```{r fig2m, fig.width=9.5, fig.height=11}
library(patchwork)
## ---- Figure 2 ---------------------------------------------------------------------
## Per site: weighted KDE (bw 0.09 ka) with its 95 % sampling (bootstrap) and age (Monte Carlo)
## envelopes, and below it every age with its 95 % range, by dating method.
## Grey shading: low-density intervals (both upper 95 % limits below the uniform density);
## coloured bars: published presence gaps, bounded by the audited ages.
meth_shape <- c("U-Th" = 16, "14C" = 17)
env_alpha  <- c("Sampling (bootstrap)" = 0.22, "Age (Monte Carlo)" = 0.5)
panel_lab  <- c(site_levels, "Regional composite")
panel_col  <- c(custom_colors[site_levels], "Regional composite" = unname(custom_colors["Regional"]))
n_lab <- recs %>% count(spot, method) %>% group_by(spot) %>%
  summarise(lab = paste0("n = ", sum(n), " (", paste(paste(n, sub("14C", "\u00b9\u2074C", method)), collapse = ", "), ")"), .groups = "drop")
n_lab <- bind_rows(n_lab, data.frame(spot = "Regional composite", lab = paste0("n = ", nrow(recs), " records, 4 sites")))

x_common <- list(scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6, minor_breaks = seq(0, 6, 0.5), expand = c(0.005, 0)),
                 coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 6)),
                 theme_classic(base_size = 12),
                 theme(plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold"), legend.position = "bottom",
                       panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "grey92", linewidth = 0.3)))

kde_panel <- function(sp, show_x = FALSE) {
  d   <- signal_all %>% filter(spot == sp)
  col <- unname(panel_col[sp])
  top <- max(d$q975, d$age_q975) * 1.05
  env <- bind_rows(
    data.frame(x = d$x, lo = d$q025, hi = d$q975, env = "Sampling (bootstrap)"),
    data.frame(x = d$x, lo = d$age_q025, hi = d$age_q975, env = "Age (Monte Carlo)"))
  env$env <- factor(env$env, names(env_alpha))
  ld  <- low_density %>% filter(spot == sp)
  sg  <- site_gaps %>% filter(spot == sp)
  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_rect(data = ld, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf), fill = "grey88") +
    geom_ribbon(data = env, aes(x, ymin = lo, ymax = hi, alpha = env), fill = col) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1 / 6, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey40") +
    geom_line(data = d, aes(x, estimate), colour = col, linewidth = 0.7) +
    scale_alpha_manual(values = env_alpha, name = "95 % envelope", drop = FALSE) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = expression("Density (ka"^-1*")"), title = sp, subtitle = n_lab$lab[n_lab$spot == sp]) +
    x_common + theme(axis.text.x = if (show_x) element_text() else element_blank(),
                     plot.title = element_text(colour = col, face = "bold", size = 13, margin = margin(b = 1)),
                     plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey30", size = 10.5, margin = margin(b = 2)))
  if (nrow(sg)) p <- p + geom_rect(data = sg, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax),
                                    ymin = top * 1.13, ymax = top * 1.2, fill = col, alpha = 0.8)
  p + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, top * 1.22), expand = c(0, 0))
}

rec_panel <- function(sp, show_x = TRUE) {
  d <- recs %>% filter(spot == sp) %>%
    mutate(method = factor(method, c("U-Th", "14C")),
           y = as.numeric(method) + (rank(t_ka, ties.method = "first") %% 4 - 1.5) * 0.12)
  ggplot(d, aes(y = y)) +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = pmax(lo95, 0), xmax = pmin(hi95, 6)), height = 0, colour = panel_col[sp],
                   alpha = 0.55, linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_point(aes(x = pmax(t_ka, 0), shape = method), colour = panel_col[sp], size = 0.9) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = meth_shape, labels = c("U-Th", "\u00b9\u2074C"), name = "Dating method", drop = FALSE) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:2, labels = c("U-Th", "\u00b9\u2074C"), limits = c(0.55, 2.45)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    x_common + theme(axis.text.x = if (show_x) element_text() else element_blank(),
                     axis.line.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
}

tags <- setNames(letters[1:5], panel_lab)
## sites in the order used by every figure of this document (site_levels)
pl <- list(kde_panel(site_levels[1]) + labs(tag = "a"), kde_panel(site_levels[2]) + labs(tag = "b"),
           rec_panel(site_levels[1]), rec_panel(site_levels[2]),
           kde_panel(site_levels[3]) + labs(tag = "c"), kde_panel(site_levels[4]) + labs(tag = "d"),
           rec_panel(site_levels[3]), rec_panel(site_levels[4]),
           kde_panel("Regional composite", show_x = TRUE) + labs(tag = "e", x = "Age (ka BP)"))
design <- "
AB
CD
EF
GH
II"
fig2 <- wrap_plots(pl, design = design, heights = c(3, 1.1, 3, 1.1, 3), guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") &
  guides(alpha = guide_legend(override.aes = list(fill = "grey30")),
         shape = guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = "grey30", size = 2)))

fig2
ggsave("Figure_2.pdf", plot = fig2, width = 9.5, height = 11, dpi = 300, device = cairo_pdf)

**Supplementary Figure S1** (`Supplementary_Figure_S1.pdf`). Sensitivity of the weighted kernel densities to the bandwidth (0.05, 0.09 and 0.15 ka), with the 95 % sampling (light) and age (dark) envelopes of each. Narrower bandwidths resolve more peaks, but the age envelope widens relative to the sampling envelope, most in the radiocarbon-dated sites. Peaks and troughs that persist at 0.15 ka are not artefacts of the smoothing choice.

```{r figS1-bandwidth, fig.width=11, fig.height=11}
bw_set <- c(0.05, 0.09, 0.15)
bw_env <- bind_rows(lapply(bw_set, function(bw) {
  set.seed(20261003)
  bind_rows(lapply(c(site_levels, "Regional composite"), function(sp) {
    reg <- sp == "Regional composite"
    i   <- if (reg) seq_len(nrow(recs)) else which(recs$spot == sp)
    w   <- if (reg) recs$w_regional else recs$w_site[i]
    st  <- if (reg) recs$spot else if (sp == "Florida") recs$source[i] else rep(1, length(i))
    smp <- calc_density_summary(recs$t_ka[i], w, sp, strata = st, B = 1000, bw = bw)$signal_df
    cbind(smp[, c("x", "estimate", "q025", "q975", "spot")], kde_age_env(i, w, bw = bw), bw = bw)
  }))
}))
bw_env$spot <- factor(bw_env$spot, panel_lab)  # site_levels, as in every figure
figS1 <- ggplot(bw_env, aes(x)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q025, ymax = q975, fill = spot), alpha = 0.22) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = age_q025, ymax = age_q975, fill = spot), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = estimate, colour = spot), linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = panel_col, guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = panel_col, guide = "none") +
  facet_grid(spot ~ paste("bandwidth", bw, "ka"), scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6, expand = c(0.005, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Age (ka BP)", y = expression("Density (ka"^-1*")")) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) + theme(strip.background = element_blank(), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
figS1
ggsave("Supplementary_Figure_S1.pdf", plot = figS1, width = 11, height = 11, dpi = 300, device = cairo_pdf)

## relative width of the envelopes (sum of 95 % ranges / sum of the estimate), by bandwidth
bw_env %>% group_by(Panel = spot, bw) %>%
  summarise(sampling = sum(q975 - q025) / sum(estimate), age = sum(age_q975 - age_q025) / sum(estimate),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(age_over_sampling = age / sampling) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))
```

### 1.5 Abundance and Holocene trends in climatic variables

Panel (a) shows the modelled series of Section 1.3: the relative abundance `counts_norm_sv` of each site per 0.1-ka bin (Florida source-standardized), stacked by site. The height of each stack is the per-bin sum from which the regional composite is normalized. Bins without records have no bar. The legend gives the number of records per site.

**Figure 3a** (`Figure_3a.pdf`). Relative abundance of *A. palmata* per 100-year interval, stacked by reef site.

```{r count-by-site}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

n_records <- table(datos_reg_pal$spot)
site_labels <- setNames(paste0(site_levels, " (n = ", n_records[site_levels], ")"), site_levels)

norm_stack <- bind_rows(datos_pm, datos_fl_std, datos_bz, datos_sc) %>%
  transmute(age, spot = factor(panel, levels = rev(site_levels)), counts_norm_sv)

pr <- ggplot(norm_stack, aes(x = age, y = counts_norm_sv, fill = spot)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", width = 0.09, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = custom_colors[site_levels], labels = site_labels,
                    breaks = site_levels) +

       y = "Relative abundance\n(stacked by site)",
       fill = "Site") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +

        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 6, 0.5), minor_breaks = seq(0, 6, 0.5)) +

pr
ggsave("Figure_3a.pdf", plot = pr, width = 9, height = 5.5, dpi = 300, device = cairo_pdf)
```

We assemble Fig. 3. Panel (a) is Fig. 3a. Below it, four panels show, for each of the 60 centennial bins:

- **(b)** the `GMHT_CPS0_30N` temperature anomaly (^o^C);
- **(c)** the centennial rate of change of the temperature anomaly (δT, ^o^C; `dT_raw`), the difference between consecutive bins of the CPS reconstruction;
- **(d)** the smoothed centennial tropical-cyclone frequency (`Hur100_av`, events per century, centred 200-year smoothing) as bars (dark grey where \> 10) and the centennial tropical-cyclone frequency (`Hur100_fqcy`) as a step line;
- **(e)** local hurricane activity in Florida (`FL_pact`): proportion of the Florida-proximal paleotempestological records that report an active interval in each bin, as bars (dark blue where ≥ 0.5, the threshold that defines the "active" regime); bins older than 3.5 ka rest on a single record (Toomey et al. 2013);
- **(f)** the nominal thermal, hydroclimatic (Yucatán and Florida series) and hurricane (Yucatán and Florida series) regimes, drawn as contiguous time segments over the full span of each bin.

**Figure 3** (`Figure_3.pdf`). Reconstruction of regional coral abundance and paleoclimate trends. The climate panels (b–f) are drawn from the 60-bin climate table, so they cover the full 0–6 ka interval, including bins without fossil records.

Before modelling, we inspect pairwise correlations among numeric variables (Section 2.1) and the distribution of abundance across combinations of climate regimes (Section 3.1.3). No predictor is removed on the basis of these analyses. Redundancy is handled instead by never entering the two hurricane metrics in the same model (Section 3.3) and by assessing overlap among smooth terms after fitting (concurvity, Section 4.2).

## **2.** Exploratory Data Analysis

#### 2.1 Variable correlation plot

We compute Pearson correlations among the four continuous climate predictors over the 60 centennial bins of the climate table (`datos_cli`), so that each bin counts once regardless of how many fossil records it contains, and cross-tabulate the three categorical regimes.

The only strong correlation is between the two hurricane metrics (Hur100_fqcy and Hur100_av, *r* = 0.90), which is why they are never entered in the same model (Section 3.3). The other correlations are weak to moderate (\|*r*\| ≤ 0.46): both hurricane metrics are negatively correlated with GMHT_CPS0_30N (*r* = −0.39 for Hur100_fqcy and −0.46 for Hur100_av), and GMHT_CPS0_30N is correlated with dT_raw at *r* = 0.36.

The categorical regimes, by contrast, are partly nested, because they are defined on the same chronology (Yucatán hydroclimate and Schmitt et al. 2025 hurricane series for the Yucatán, Belize and Saint Croix panels and the regional composite; Florida series for the Florida panel):

- **Yucatán hydroclimate.** LIA bins are all wet (6 of 6) and "warmer" bins are never dry (6 wet, 7 without data); CWP&MWA bins are mostly dry (5 of 6). The 20 bins without hydroclimate data all fall in the "cooler" or "warmer" regimes and under low or moderate hurricane activity.
- **Hurricane regime (Schmitt et al. 2025).** "calm" occurs only within LIA (4 of 4 bins), "enhanced" mostly within CWP&MWA (5 of 7), "low" only within the "cooler" and "warmer" regimes, and "high" in two bins (LIA and warmer).
- **Florida series.** The Florida hydroclimate is wet only within the "cooler" regime (18 of 35 bins); all CWP&MWA, LIA and "warmer" bins are dry. All "warmer" bins are quiet in the Florida hurricane series.

With the current data no combined candidate is rank-deficient (Section 3.3), but the nesting means that regime contrasts are partly confounded with one another (for example, LIA with the wet Yucatán hydroclimate and with the calm hurricane regime) and must be read jointly.

**Supplementary Figure S2.** Pearson correlation matrix of the continuous climate predictors across the 60 centennial bins.

```{r corr, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=7.5}
library(corrplot)

clim_vars  <- c("GMHT_CPS0_30N", "dT_raw", "Hur100_fqcy", "Hur100_av")
cor_matrix <- cor(datos_cli[, clim_vars])

corrplot(cor_matrix, method = "circle", type = "upper",
         tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45, addCoef.col = "black")

pdf("Supplementary_Figure_S2.pdf", width = 8.5, height = 7.5, pointsize = 15)
corrplot(cor_matrix, method = "circle", type = "upper",
         tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45, addCoef.col = "black")
invisible(dev.off())

## regime nesting (NA = bins without hydroclimate data)
table(Thermal = datos_cli$Thermal, Hydro = datos_cli$Hydro, useNA = "ifany")
table(Thermal = datos_cli$Thermal, Hurricane = datos_cli$Hurricane)
table(Hydro = datos_cli$Hydro, Hurricane = datos_cli$Hurricane, useNA = "ifany")
## Florida series
table(Thermal = datos_cli$Thermal, Hydro_FL = datos_cli$Hydro_FL)
table(Thermal = datos_cli$Thermal, Hur_FL = datos_cli$Hur_FL)
```

## 3. GAM analysis

### 3.1 Modelling data

All models use `merged_df_g`, built in Section 1.3: the source-standardized Florida series, the three single-source site series and the regional composite. The two subsections below assess the Florida source standardization, and Section 3.1.3 describes abundance across climate-regime combinations.

#### 3.1.1 Florida: pooled normalization (sensitivity series)

`datos_fl_norm` applies the same procedure to Florida without source standardization, pooling records across sources before normalization. This series is used in the comparison of Section 3.1.2 and in the sensitivity analysis of Section 4.5, where the selected Florida models are refitted to it; it is not used in model selection.

```{r fl-norm-function}

normalize_counts <- function(df, panel_name){
  df %>%
    mutate(
      counts_norm = round(counts / max(counts, na.rm = TRUE), 4),
      # aplicar SV si hay 0 o 1
      counts_norm_sv = ifelse(counts_norm %in% c(0,1),
                              ((counts_norm * (n() - 1)) + 0.5) / n(),
                              counts_norm),
      panel = panel_name
    )
}

datos_fl_norm <- merged_df %>%
  filter(spot == "Florida") %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(
    counts = sum(counts, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_av = mean(Hur100_av, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hur100_fqcy = mean(Hur100_fqcy, na.rm = TRUE),
    GMHT_CPS0_30N = mean(GMHT_CPS0_30N, na.rm = TRUE),
    dT_raw = mean(dT_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hydro = first(Hydro),
    Thermal = first(Thermal),
    Hurricane = first(Hurricane),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  normalize_counts("Florida")
```

#### 3.1.2 Florida: effect of source standardization

##### a. Comparison table

We join the pooled series (`norm`) and the source-standardized series (`std`) by bin into `fl_compare`.

```{r florida-comparison}
fl_compare <- full_join(

  datos_fl_norm %>%
    select(age, counts_norm_sv) %>%
    rename(norm = counts_norm_sv),

  datos_fl_std %>%
    select(age, counts_norm_sv) %>%
    rename(std = counts_norm_sv),

  by = "age"

)
```

##### b. Quick assessment

We summarize the differences (std − norm), list the 20 largest, compute the correlation between the two series, and plot both series and their difference.

```{r florida-comparison-visual}

summary(fl_compare$std - fl_compare$norm)

max(abs(fl_compare$std - fl_compare$norm),
    na.rm = TRUE)

fl_compare <- fl_compare %>%
  mutate(
    delta = std - norm
  )

fl_compare %>%
  mutate(
    delta = std - norm,
    abs_delta = abs(delta)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs_delta)) %>%
  select(age, norm, std, delta) %>%
  slice(1:20)


cor(
  fl_compare$norm,
  fl_compare$std,
  use = "complete.obs"
)


p_fl_a <- ggplot(fl_compare, aes(age)) +
  
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      ymin = pmin(norm, std),
      ymax = pmax(norm, std)
    ),
    fill = "grey70",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  
  geom_line(
    aes(y = norm,
        colour = "Original"),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  
  geom_line(
    aes(y = std,
        colour = "Standardized"),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Original" = "black",
      "Standardized" = "red"
    )
  ) +
  
  scale_x_reverse() +
  
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  
  labs(
    x = "Age (ka BP)",
    y = "Relative abundance",
    colour = NULL
  )

p_fl_b <- ggplot(
  fl_compare,
  aes(age, delta)
) +
  
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = 2
  ) +
  
  geom_area(
    fill = "steelblue",
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  
  scale_x_reverse() +
  
  labs(
    x = "Age (ka BP)",
    y = "Standardized - Original"
  ) +
  
  theme_bw(base_size = 15)

library(patchwork)
figS3 <- p_fl_a / p_fl_b + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "a")
figS3
ggsave("Supplementary_Figure_S3.pdf", plot = figS3, width = 9, height = 9, dpi = 300, device = cairo_pdf)
```

The differences have a median of 0.100, a mean of 0.121 and a range of −0.211 to 0.489. The largest occur at 2.5, 3.3 and 5.9–6.0 ka. The two series are correlated at *r* = 0.794. Source standardization therefore preserves the overall temporal pattern but raises relative abundance in most bins (13 of the 44 differences, 30 %, are negative), most strongly at 2.4–2.5, 3.2–3.3 and 5.9–6.0 ka. This comparison concerns the response series; the GAMs refitted to the pooled series are compared with the source-standardized ones in Section 4.5.

**Supplementary Figure S3.** (a) Pooled (black) and source-standardized (red) Florida series; the grey band marks their difference. (b) Difference std − norm. Age is in ka.

#### **3.1.3 *Acropora palmata* abundance across climate-regime combinations**

We combine the three regime labels into `ClimateCombo` (Thermal_Hydro_Hurricane) and tabulate their frequency per panel (**Supplementary Table S3**; each panel block ends with its number of bins). The regional composite is one of the panels, so its bins are not additional observations. No missing values occur.

We then retain combinations observed in at least three bins in at least one panel. Because the filter is applied across panels, a retained combination can still have *n* = 1–2 in a given panel (e.g. LIA_wet_calm, *n* = 1 in Belize; warmer_wet_low, *n* = 1 in Punta Maroma). Nine combinations are excluded, each with one or two bins per panel: cooler_dry_enhanced, CWP&MWA_dry_quiet, LIA_dry_active, LIA_dry_quiet, CWP&MWA_wet_enhanced, LIA_wet_enhanced, CWP&MWA_dry_moderate, LIA_wet_high and warmer_wet_high. The filter retains 27 of 31 bins in Punta Maroma, 40 of 44 in Florida, 20 of 24 in Belize, 15 of 19 in Saint Croix and 51 of 57 in the regional composite.

The filter excludes the youngest bin (0–0.1 ka). Its combination, warmer_wet_high, occurs in a single bin, and this bin holds the maximum relative abundance in Punta Maroma (0.98), Saint Croix (0.97) and the regional composite (0.99), and one of the highest values in Belize (0.75; maximum 0.98). Supplementary Table S4 and Supplementary Figure S4 therefore describe abundance across regimes *excluding* the modern peak; that peak is shown in Figs. 2 and 3, and its influence on the models is assessed by refitting them without it (Section 4.5).

**Supplementary Table S4** gives *n*, mean, SD and range of `counts_norm_sv` for each panel and retained combination. A panel-level summary (`resumen_panel`) is also computed but not shown.

##### Climate combinations (frequencies)

```{r climate-combinations}

library(forcats)
eda_counts <- merged_df_g %>%
  
  mutate(
    ClimateCombo = interaction(
      Thermal,
      Hydro,
      Hurricane,
      sep = "_"
    )
  )

eda_counts[!complete.cases(eda_counts), ]

eda_counts$ClimateCombo <- reorder(
  eda_counts$ClimateCombo,
  eda_counts$counts_norm_sv,
  median
)

combo_freq <- eda_counts %>%
  count(panel, ClimateCombo)

combo_freq_tbl <- combo_freq %>%
  mutate(ClimateCombo = as.character(ClimateCombo)) %>%
  group_by(panel) %>%
  group_modify(~ bind_rows(.x, tibble::tibble(ClimateCombo = "Total", n = sum(.x$n)))) %>%
  ungroup()

tab_S3 <- combo_freq_tbl %>%
  gt(groupname_col = "panel") %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Climate combinations (frequencies)",
    subtitle = "Number of centennial bins per panel and climatic combination"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = n, decimals = 0) %>%
  cols_label(ClimateCombo = "Climate combination", n = "Bins") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_body(rows = ClimateCombo == "Total"))

tab_S3
gt::gtsave(tab_S3, "Supplementary_Table_S3.docx")
```

##### Climate-combination summary

```{r climate-combination-summary}
combos_validos <- combo_freq %>%
  filter(n >= 3) %>%
  pull(ClimateCombo) %>%
  as.character() %>%
  unique()

## excluded combinations and the bins they leave out of Table S4 / Fig. S4
combo_freq %>% filter(!as.character(ClimateCombo) %in% combos_validos) %>%
  group_by(ClimateCombo) %>% summarise(bins = paste(panel, n, collapse = "; "), .groups = "drop")
eda_counts %>% group_by(panel) %>%
  summarise(bins = n(), retained = sum(as.character(ClimateCombo) %in% combos_validos), .groups = "drop")

invisible(
  combo_freq %>%
    filter(n >= 3)
)

invisible(
  combo_freq %>%
    filter(n < 3)
)

datos_filtrados <- eda_counts %>%
  filter(
    ClimateCombo %in% combos_validos
  )

datos_filtrados <- datos_filtrados %>%
  group_by(panel) %>%
  mutate(
    ClimateCombo = fct_reorder(
      ClimateCombo,
      counts_norm_sv,
      .fun = median
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

resumen_panel <- datos_filtrados %>%
  group_by(panel) %>%
  summarise(
    n_obs = n(),
    mean_abund = mean(counts_norm_sv, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_abund = sd(counts_norm_sv, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_abund = min(counts_norm_sv, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_abund = max(counts_norm_sv, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

resumen_panel_combo <- datos_filtrados %>%
  group_by(
    panel,
    ClimateCombo
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    n_obs = n(),
    mean_abund = mean(counts_norm_sv, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_abund = sd(counts_norm_sv, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_abund = min(counts_norm_sv, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_abund = max(counts_norm_sv, na.rm = TRUE),

In Saint Croix the response takes essentially two values: 13 of the 15 retained bins hold a single record (0.50), so differences among combinations rest on two bins with two records each (CWP&MWA_dry_enhanced and warmer_wet_low). Most combinations are represented by fewer than five bins per panel, so these patterns are descriptive only.

### 3.2. Marginal GAM effects analysis

Relative abundance is continuous and bounded in (0, 1), so we fit GAMs with a beta distribution and logit link (`mgcv::gam`, family `betar`). Smoothing parameters are estimated by REML. Continuous predictors enter as thin-plate regression splines (mgcv default, basis dimension *k* = 10).

Climate regimes enter as factors with reference levels "warmer" (Thermal), "wet" (Hydro) and "low" (Hurricane). Their coefficients are contrasts on the logit scale relative to the reference, conditional on the other terms. Every model includes a smooth of age, `s(age)`, which absorbs temporal structure not attributed to the climate predictor.

Modelling proceeds in two stages: marginal models, with `s(age)` plus one climate predictor (this section), and combined models, a nested sequence with two branches, one per hurricane metric (Section 3.3).

Candidates are ranked by AIC, ΔAIC and Akaike weights; models within ΔAIC ≤ 2 of the best are considered competitive. Marginal models are fitted without `select = TRUE` and with *k* = 10, whereas combined models use `select = TRUE` and a reduced *k*; AIC values are therefore not comparable between the two stages.

In this document, "linear" models are those whose climate term is a categorical factor (a parametric term), and "smooth" models those whose climate term is a continuous predictor fitted as a spline.

#### 3.2.1 Candidate models

`formulas_mg` defines seven marginal candidates, each consisting of `s(age)` plus one of: `s(GMHT_CPS0_30N)` (M_temp), `s(dT_raw)` (M_dt), `s(Hur100_fqcy)` (M_hf), `s(Hur100_av)` (M_hav), Thermal (M_the), Hydro (M_hyd) or Hurricane (M_hur). `fit_gams_panel()` fits all candidates to one panel, and `compare_gams()` returns AIC, ΔAIC and Akaike weights.

**Hydroclimate in panels with gaps in its series.** The Yucatán hydroclimate series, used for Punta Maroma, Belize, Saint Croix and the regional composite, has no data for 20 of the 60 bins (level "no data"). That level is not a climatic state: as a factor level it contrasts periods with and without a hydroclimate record, and in preliminary fits it produced effects that had no climatic meaning (e.g. Saint Croix, where the hydroclimate model ranked first only through the "no data" contrast). In every panel whose series has such bins, the Hydro term is therefore removed from all candidates (`drop_hydro()`): M_hyd is not fitted, and in the combined sequence (Section 3.3) M5 is dropped and M6 and M7 keep the thermal and hurricane regimes without Hydro. Florida, whose hydroclimate series has no gaps, keeps all candidates. The marginal comparison therefore involves six candidates in Punta Maroma, Belize, Saint Croix and the regional composite, and seven in Florida.

```{r setup-formulas}
formulas_mg <- list(
  M_temp = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(GMHT_CPS0_30N),
  M_dt   = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(dT_raw),          
  M_hf   = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(Hur100_fqcy),
  M_hav  = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + s(Hur100_av),
  M_the  = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + Thermal,
  M_hyd  = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + Hydro,
  M_hur  = counts_norm_sv ~ s(age) + Hurricane
)

## ---- Hydroclimate in panels with gaps in its series ---------------------------------
## The Yucatán hydroclimate series (used for Punta Maroma, Belize, Saint Croix and the
## regional composite) has no data for part of the record (level "no data"). That level is
## not a climatic state: as a factor level it contrasts periods with and without a
## hydroclimate record and can produce spurious effects. In any panel whose series has
## such bins, the Hydro term is therefore removed from every candidate; candidates that
## become duplicates of another (M5 = M4) or lose their only climate term (M_hyd) are
## dropped, and M6 / M7 keep the thermal and hurricane regimes without Hydro. Florida,
## whose hydroclimate series has no gaps, keeps all candidates.
hydro_has_gaps <- function(data) any(as.character(data$Hydro) == "no data", na.rm = TRUE)
drop_hydro <- function(formulas, data) {
  if (!hydro_has_gaps(data)) return(formulas)
  has_h <- vapply(formulas, function(f) "Hydro" %in% all.vars(f), logical(1))
  red   <- lapply(formulas, function(f) if ("Hydro" %in% all.vars(f)) update(f, . ~ . - Hydro) else f)
  key   <- vapply(red, function(f) paste(sort(attr(terms(f), "term.labels")), collapse = " + "), "")
  red[!(has_h & (duplicated(key) | key == "s(age)"))]
}

fit_gams_panel <- function(data, formulas) {
  formulas <- drop_hydro(formulas, data)
  lapply(formulas, function(f)
    gam(f, data = data, family = betar(link = "logit"), method = "REML"))
}

compare_gams <- function(fits) {
  stats <- lapply(fits, AIC)
  df <- data.frame(Model = names(stats), AIC = unlist(stats))
  df <- df %>%
    mutate(deltaAIC = AIC - min(AIC),
           weight = exp(-0.5 * deltaAIC) / sum(exp(-0.5 * deltaAIC)))
  return(df)
}
```

#### 3.2.2 Model competition (ΔAIC and Akaike weights)

We fit the seven candidates to each panel of `merged_df_g` and plot ΔAIC and Akaike weights by panel.

Information-theoretic comparison of the marginal GAMs by panel.** (a) ΔAIC of each candidate (Supplementary Table S5); the red dashed line marks ΔAIC = 2, and the ΔAIC axis is scaled separately for each panel. (b) Akaike weights, on a common 0–1 scale. Candidates are listed in the same order in every panel.

panels <- unique(merged_df_g$panel)

results <- lapply(panels, function(p) {
  
  df_panel <- merged_df_g %>%
    filter(panel == p)
  
  if(nrow(df_panel) < 3 ||
     all(is.na(df_panel$counts_norm_sv)))
    return(NULL)
  
  fits <- fit_gams_panel(
    df_panel,
    formulas_mg
  )
  
  stats <- compare_gams(fits)
  
  stats$panel <- p
  
  stats
  
})

library(patchwork)

site_order <- c("Punta Maroma", "Florida", "Belize", "Saint Croix", "Regional")

plot_model_selection <- function(stats, panel_var, model_levels) {
  d <- stats %>%
    mutate(Panel = factor(.data[[panel_var]], levels = site_order),
           Model = factor(Model, levels = rev(model_levels)))
  base <- function(yvar, ylab) {
    ggplot(d, aes(x = Model, y = .data[[yvar]], colour = Panel)) +
      geom_segment(aes(xend = Model, y = 0, yend = .data[[yvar]]), linewidth = 0.8) +
      geom_point(size = 2.2) +
      coord_flip() +
      scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = custom_colors[site_order], guide = "none") +
      labs(x = NULL, y = ylab) +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
      theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
            panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
  }
  p_d <- base("deltaAIC", "ΔAIC") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 2, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
    facet_wrap(~Panel, nrow = 1, drop = FALSE, scales = "free_x")
  p_w <- base("weight", "Akaike weight") +
    facet_wrap(~Panel, nrow = 1, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1))
  (p_d / p_w) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "a")
}

#### 3.2.3 Marginal GAM model ranking

**Supplementary Table S5. Marginal GAM ranking by panel.** For each panel, the seven candidates are ordered by AIC, with ΔAIC, Akaike weight and rank. (`get_best_models()` refits the same models as Section 3.2.2 on the same data.)

```{r best-gams}

linear_models <- c(
  "M_the",
  "M_hyd",
  "M_hur"
)

smooth_models <- c(
  "M_temp",
  "M_dt",
  "M_hf",
  "M_hav"
)

get_best_models <- function(data, formulas){
  
  fits <- fit_gams_panel(data, formulas)
  
  ranking <- compare_gams(fits) %>%
    arrange(AIC) %>%
    mutate(
      Rank = row_number()
    )
  
  best_linear <- ranking %>%
    filter(Model %in% linear_models) %>%
    slice_min(AIC, n = 1)
  
  best_smooth <- ranking %>%
    filter(Model %in% smooth_models) %>%
    slice_min(AIC, n = 1)
  
  list(
    fits = fits,
    ranking = ranking,
    best_linear = best_linear,
    best_smooth = best_smooth
  )
  
}

        formulas[[smo_name]],
        data = data,

  )
  
}

We then extract, for each of these models: AIC, deviance explained and adjusted R²; the climate term with the lowest term-level *p*-value (`s(age)` excluded) and that *p*-value; the factor contrasts with *p* \< 0.05; the EDF of each smooth; and a support label ("Supported" if the term-level climate *p* \< 0.05, otherwise "Weak support"). Term-level *p*-values come from a joint Wald test of the whole term (`anova()`): for a categorical regime, all levels are tested together; for a continuous predictor, the spline is tested. Contrasts are relative to the reference levels warmer / wet / low. *p*-values below 10⁻⁴ are reported as "\<1e-04", the precision limit of mgcv's approximation for smooth terms.

**Table 1. Best-supported marginal GAMs by panel.** Highest-ranked categorical-regime (linear) and continuous-climate (smooth) models, with model fit, climate term with the lowest term-level *p*-value, significant contrasts versus the reference level, EDF of the smooth terms and support label.

```{r comparison-table}
library(webshot2)
extract_gam_stats <- function(model, panel, model_type, model_name,
                              alpha = 0.05, p_floor = 1e-4) {
  
  sm <- summary(model)
  av <- anova(model)                       # term-level Wald tests
  
  ## 1. Climate p-values at TERM level (s(age) excluded)
  # Parametric terms: one joint test per factor (all levels together)
  pt_tab <- av$pTerms.table
  p_par  <- if (!is.null(pt_tab) && NROW(pt_tab) > 0)
    setNames(pt_tab[, "p-value"], rownames(pt_tab)) else numeric(0)
  # Smooth terms
  st_tab <- sm$s.table
  st_cl  <- st_tab[rownames(st_tab) != "s(age)", , drop = FALSE]
  p_smo  <- setNames(st_cl[, "p-value"], rownames(st_cl))
  
  p_all  <- c(p_par, p_smo)
  p_all  <- p_all[!is.na(p_all)]
  # mgcv's smooth p-values are approximations; values below ~1e-4 (or slightly
  # negative, from rounding) are not meaningful beyond "very small"
  p_all  <- pmax(p_all, 0)
  
  climate_p   <- if (length(p_all)) min(p_all) else NA_real_
  climate_trm <- if (length(p_all)) names(p_all)[which.min(p_all)] else NA_character_
  sig_terms   <- names(p_all)[p_all < alpha]
  
  ## 2. Significant factor CONTRASTS vs. the reference level (for interpretation)
  ptab  <- sm$p.table
  contr <- ptab[rownames(ptab) != "(Intercept)", , drop = FALSE]
  contr <- contr[!is.na(contr[, 4]) & contr[, 4] < alpha, , drop = FALSE]
  sig_contr <- if (NROW(contr))
    paste0(rownames(contr), " (", sprintf("%.2f", contr[, 1]),
           ", p=", format.pval(contr[, 4], digits = 2, eps = p_floor), ")",
           collapse = "; ") else if (NROW(ptab) <= 1) "n/a (no categorical terms)" else "none"
  
  data.frame(
    Panel             = panel,
    Type              = model_type,
    Model             = model_name,
    AIC               = round(AIC(model), 3),
    DevianceExplained = round(sm$dev.expl, 3),
    R2_Adj            = round(sm$r.sq, 3),
    ClimateTerm       = climate_trm,
    Climate_p         = climate_p,
    Climate_p_label   = if (is.na(climate_p)) "NA" else
      format.pval(climate_p, digits = 2, eps = p_floor),
    SignificantTerms  = if (length(sig_terms)) paste(sig_terms, collapse = "; ")
    else "Not significant",
    SignificantContrasts = sig_contr,
    EDF_Terms         = paste0(rownames(st_tab), " (EDF=",
                               round(st_tab[, "edf"], 2), ")", collapse = "; "),
    Inference         = ifelse(!is.na(climate_p) && climate_p < alpha,
                               "Supported", "Weak support"),
    stringsAsFactors  = FALSE
  )
}

model_labels <- c(
  M_the = "Thermal regime",
  M_hyd = "Hydroclimatic trends",
  M_hur = "Hurricane regime",
  M_temp = "GMHT anomalies",
  M_dt = "thermal rate of change δT",
  M_hf = "TC frequency",
  M_hav = "Smoothed TC frequency"

build_panel_summary <- function(best_obj,
                                panel_name,
                                formulas,
                                data){
  
  lin_name <- best_obj$best_linear$Model
  smo_name <- best_obj$best_smooth$Model
  
  lin_model <- gam(
    formulas[[lin_name]],
    data = data,
    family = betar(link="logit"),
    method = "REML"
  )
  
  smo_model <- gam(
    formulas[[smo_name]],
    data = data,
    family = betar(link="logit"),
    method = "REML"
  )
  
  bind_rows(
    
    extract_gam_stats(
      lin_model,
      panel_name,
      "Linear",
      lin_name
    ),
    
    extract_gam_stats(
      smo_model,
      panel_name,
      "Smooth",
      smo_name
    )
    
  )
}

    "Belize",
    formulas_mg,

    best_sc,
    "Saint Croix",
    formulas_mg,

    best_reg,
    "Regional",
    formulas_mg,
    datos_reg
  )
  
)
